youtube.title: How Functions Work in Rust (fn, parameters, return) 🦀 | Rust Day 9 #Shorts

scenes.say: No return keyword, yet this function returns five. Here's how Rust functions work.

scenes.heading: Your first function
scenes.say: F N starts a function, named in snake case. Each parameter needs a type: a and b are i32. The arrow i32 means it gives back an i32. The last line, a plus b, has no semicolon, so it's the return value. In main, we call add with two and three.
scenes.captions: fn starts a function, named in snake_case. Each parameter needs a type: a and b are i32. The arrow -> i32 means it gives back an i32. The last line, a + b, has no semicolon, so it's the return value. In main, we call add(2, 3).

scenes.heading: What happens
scenes.say: Two and three go in as a and b. a plus b makes five, which comes back out into sum. And add sits below main: Rust doesn't mind.
scenes.captions: 2 and 3 go in as a and b. a + b makes 5, which comes back out into sum. And add sits below main: Rust doesn't mind.

scenes.heading: Common mistake
scenes.say: Now the classic beginner mistake: forgetting the return type.

scenes.heading: The compiler helps
scenes.caption: try adding -> i32
scenes.say: Mismatched types: expected empty parentheses, which means nothing, but found an i32. And the fix is right there: add arrow i32.
scenes.captions: Mismatched types: expected (), which means nothing, but found an i32. And the fix is right there: add -> i32.

scenes.heading: Why types are required
scenes.say: Why so strict? With types in the signature, the compiler checks every call, and you almost never need type labels anywhere else.

scenes.heading: Recap
scenes.say: Recap: F N, a name, typed parameters, an arrow for the return type, and the last expression is the result.
scenes.captions: Recap: fn, a name, typed parameters, an arrow for the return type, and the last expression is the result.
